newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Thousands rally across Australia against racism.
newsitem.headline: Thousands rally across Australia against racism.

text.p: Thousands of Australians concerned at signs of growing racism held protest rallies in four centres across the country on Saturday in a backlash against the views of maverick politician Pauline Hanson.
More than 5,000 people turned out for the biggest rally in Sydney where a coalition of mainly Asian ethnic groups and trade unions joined a march on the prime minister's office.

Prime Minister John Howard, who is attending an Asia-Pacific summit in Manila, has been accused of not taking a strong enough stand against Hanson, whose views against Asian immigration and aboriginal welfare have struck a chord with voters.
The crowd filled two city blocks and shouted "Hanson, Howard racist cowards -- deport Hanson not refugees" as it marched in heavy rain through the city.

Placards read "Pauline, racist, should apologise" and "Asians welcome, kick out the racists" in the procession, which was led by Korean percussionists and included representatives of the city's large Vietnamese community.
Sydney deputy mayor Henry Tsang told the rally that Asian communities had felt a surge of racial hatred since Hanson first aired her views in parliament after the election in March.
Tsang's comments followed a Sydney newspaper survey showing racial abuse against Chinese Australians had doubled in recent months, with many being spat at or physically threatened.
"I want to send a message to Hanson and her likes, whether you like it or not, multiculturalism is here to stay," Korean community spokesman Keith Kwan told the rally before the march.
This week visiting U.S. President Bill Clinton praised Sydney, host of the 2000 Olympic Games, as a model of cultural diversity and harmony.

Anti-racist rallies were also held on Saturday in the capital Canberra, the western city of Perth and in Hanson's own home town of Ipswich, in the conservative state of Queensland, where she has been hailed as a hero by supporters.
Around 1,000 people rallied in Perth and hundreds more in Canberra and Ipswich, local media reported.
A spokesman for Campaign Against Racism, organiser of the rallies, said Howard had failed to distance himself from Hanson and others who wanted slower Asian immigration.

"People generally do not accept the kind of ideas put forward by the likes of Pauline Hanson...Australians Against Further Immigration and even, I think, you could add to that list John Howard," spokesman Gordon Hewitt said.
Howard has consistenty spoken against calls for a racially based immigration policy, but has been reluctant to reply directly to what he has termed the views of one legislator.
His stance has been criticised in Asian newspapers and has begun to intrude on Canberra's relations with the region.

On Thursday, Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi raised the issue with his Australian counterpart, Alexander Downer, in the Philippines capital ahead of the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
